messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 33
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: Oceania
  relationship_status: Divorced
  occupation: Network Engineer
  trauma_type: Child's life-threatening illness
  pcl5: 44

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Arguments: Arguments, Known People: Related people, Medical Procedures: Undergoing a medical examination or procedure
  Threat: Alert at Home: I feel on guard even inside my own home, Startle to Movement: Unexpected movement nearby causes me to react as if I am in danger, Physical Reactivity: Having strong physical reactions when something reminded you of the stressful experience

Active components (must all appear in the vignette, even if not causally connected):
  - Triggers
  - Threat

Required causal connections — the vignette must convey each of these within a paragraph:
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Threat → Triggers

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Mereana had once thought of herself as the kind of person who handled crisis well. At 33, working as a network engineer, she was used to troubleshooting systems under pressure, to staying calm while other people panicked. That certainty changed during the winter her six-year-old son became critically ill. What began as a fever and lethargy escalated quickly into an emergency admission, and within days she was spending long nights under fluorescent hospital lights, watching him attached to monitors, hearing the clipped voices of clinicians discussing tests and procedures she could not bear to understand. The worst moments were the examinations and invasive procedures, when strangers leaned over her child and the room filled with the sounds of equipment, his cry, and her own helpless pleading. Even now, she can name those scenes with painful clarity, as though they happened yesterday rather than months ago.

Since then, certain moments have started to feel dangerous in themselves. Arguments, even ordinary ones, immediately put her on edge, because during the hospitalization any disagreement among staff or between relatives seemed to herald bad news, and she had learned to brace herself when voices sharpened. Related people can have the same effect: a text from her son’s father, a call from her ex-husband, or even a family member asking too directly about the boy can send her mind back to the hospital and leave her tense before she has fully registered why. Medical procedures are especially potent. A routine pediatric appointment, a blood draw, or even the sight of a white coat can make her body react as if the emergency were happening again, because those were the moments when she felt most powerless and most afraid of losing her child. Mereana has come to believe that if something can change in a child’s health once, it can change without warning again, and that belief keeps her scanning for danger long before anyone else notices anything amiss.

That vigilance has spread into everyday life. At home, she feels on guard even inside her own house, checking doors twice, listening hard when footsteps approach the bedroom, and sitting up too quickly if there is an unexpected movement nearby. A child darting past her in the hallway or a sudden noise from the kitchen can make her flinch as if she is in immediate danger. She notices her body first—her heart racing, her stomach dropping, a sharp physical surge that feels embarrassingly out of proportion—but to her it makes sense: if she stays alert enough, she may catch the next emergency before it overwhelms her. Her mind has learned to treat ordinary moments as warning signs. In the quiet of the evening, after her son is asleep, she still finds herself listening for changes in his breathing through the baby monitor she cannot quite stop using, even though he is no longer a baby. When her ex-husband calls to discuss schedules, she hears not just the call but the old possibility of news she cannot control, and the conversation leaves her shaking and keyed up long after it ends.

Over the months, this state of constant alertness has narrowed her world. She has begun avoiding arguments where she can, ending conversations quickly, and keeping interactions with relatives brief so no one asks too many questions about her son’s health. At work, she has stayed remote whenever possible, partly because she can control her environment better there, but also because being in shared spaces makes her feel exposed, as though another unexpected movement or sudden complaint could set her body off again. The distance has protected her in some ways, but it has also made her more isolated, and she has noticed that her marriage ended under the strain of all of it. She does not describe the divorce angrily; she describes it as something that happened while she was trying to keep functioning, while everyone else seemed to want answers she could not give.

Mereana came to treatment after realizing that the loop had begun to govern her days. The more she felt on guard, the more she interpreted arguments, familiar voices, and medical settings as signs that danger was close; the more those situations triggered her, the more certain she became that she could never fully relax, even at home. She sought help after a recent pediatric follow-up left her sweating, trembling, and unable to settle for the rest of the day, and after her son asked why she “looked scared all the time.” What she wants most is to stop reacting as if every sudden movement or raised voice means catastrophe is about to happen. What frightens her most is that, unless something changes, she will remain trapped in the role of watcher and guard, unable to feel safe with the child she worked so hard to keep alive.
